title: Raoul Wallenberg in Budapest
text:
In the spring and summer of 1944 hundreds of thousands of Hungarian Jews were deported to Auschwitz. In July, Raoul Wallenberg, a young Swedish businessman with no diplomatic experience, arrived in Budapest as a secretary at the Swedish legation. His mission, backed by the American War Refugee Board, was to save as many of the remaining Jews as he could.

He worked by improvising within the bureaucracy. He designed an official-looking Swedish protective passport, the Schutz-Pass, in blue and yellow with the Swedish crown, and issued thousands of them. He rented buildings around the city, hung Swedish flags on them and declared them Swedish territory, sheltering people inside. He bribed, bluffed and threatened Hungarian and German officials, and recruited hundreds of staff.

When the Arrow Cross took power in October and deportations and death marches resumed, Wallenberg went to railway stations and to the marching columns himself, handing out passes and pulling people out by insisting they were under Swedish protection.

In January 1945, as the Soviet army took Budapest, he was detained by Soviet officials and disappeared. The Soviet Union later claimed he died in a Moscow prison in 1947. The exact number of people he saved is uncertain, but it is counted in the thousands at least.
lesson: Creativity and nerve inside an existing system can achieve what direct force cannot. Use every tool your position gives you.
source: Swedish Foreign Ministry records; Yad Vashem; reports of the US War Refugee Board
caveat: Estimates of the number of people he saved vary widely, and the circumstances of his death remain unresolved.
